summary: Defines the loc-src parameter for the SIP Geolocation header field so the entity that added a location value can be identified. When there are several location values, recipients can choose which to look at first.

plainLanguage.summary: When several notes say where someone is, a name tag on each note shows who wrote it.

how to tell who added a sip location

subtitle: A small parameter that tells a SIP recipient which node added a location to a call.

tldr.problem: A SIP Geolocation header field can carry several location values, and the order alone does not say which node added each one.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8787 defines a loc-src parameter that carries the hostname of the SIP intermediary that added a location value. User agents must not insert it, and it is meant for trusted networks only.
tldr.outcome: Recipients can pick which location to look at first based on who supplied it. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 6442.

facts.label: Value
facts.value: A fully qualified hostname, not an IP address

facts.label: Registry
facts.value: SIP header field parameters, for Geolocation

today: RFC 8787 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 6442.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6442 defines the Geolocation SIP header field, which says that a message carries location information. It also says that SIP intermediaries should not add a locationValue to a request that already has one, and that an intermediary which does add location is fully responsible for any 424 (Bad Location Information) response.

Some architectures, such as those from 3GPP and ETSI, prefer location supplied by edge proxies or core-network nodes before location supplied only by the user equipment (UE). To do that, the recipient has to tell apart the node that added a value from the UE.

RFC 8787 meets that need with one new header field parameter, loc-src, in which the adding entity identifies itself by hostname. How the entity obtains the location is out of scope, and the parameter does not change the subject of the locationValue.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a phone call carries more than one note about where the caller is. This document adds a way to write down who wrote each note.

sections.title: Why Identify the Source
sections.content:
RFC 6442 says locationValues appear in the order they were added. That tells the recipient which values were added earlier in the chain, but not which node added them. Knowing the adder lets the recipient choose which location to consider first instead of relying only on order.

The stated primary use is emergency calling. Various SIP emergency architectures let the UE give location, and many also attach other sources to check veracity, to act as backup or to serve as the primary location. The RFC does not comment on those architectures. The ETSI emergency caller location architecture is given as an example where the parameter makes sense.

The parameter applies inside one private administrative domain, or between domains that have a trust relationship, meaning trust domains where Spec(T) from RFC 3325 exists. It is not included in a message sent to another network without that trust, and it is not applicable where the domain handles emergency calls without generating any location.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a pile of notes about where a lost child is. Knowing whether a teacher or a stranger wrote each one helps you choose which to read first.

sections.title: The loc-src Parameter
sections.content:
The parameter is a geoloc-param attached to a locationValue. Its ABNF is location-source = "loc-src" EQUAL hostname, where hostname is the one defined in RFC 3261.

Only a fully qualified host name is valid. IP addresses are not supported, and an entity that follows this specification and receives a loc-src containing an IP address MUST remove the parameter.

  • A conformant SIP intermediary that adds a locationValue SHOULD also add loc-src, so it is clearly identified as the node that added the location.
  • A User Agent (UA) MUST NOT insert loc-src.
  • An intermediary that receives a message from an untrusted source with loc-src set MUST remove it before passing the message into a trusted network.
sections.plainLanguage: The name tag must be a full name, not a phone number. Only helpers in the middle may write a name tag, and anyone who finds a tag from a stranger must tear it off.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
The RFC shows a SIP INVITE whose Geolocation header field has two locationValues. The first is a cid: URI, a content-indirection URI per RFC 4483, that points to a PIDF-LO location object in the SIP body, and it comes from the UE. The second is an https URI supplied by a SIP intermediary, which marks itself with loc-src=edgeproxy.example.com.

The first value has no loc-src, consistent with the rule that a UA does not insert one. A recipient that prefers network-provided location can use the tag to find the second value.
sections.plainLanguage: One note has no name tag because the phone wrote it. The other has a tag reading edgeproxy, so you know a helper in the middle wrote it.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
On privacy, the RFC says it changes none of the considerations in RFC 6442. Naming the adder exposes little more than adding a proxy identity to the Record-Route header field does (privacy for that is covered in RFC 3323).

On security, the recipient should use the parameter only in a trusted network. Adding it in an untrusted network just gives location information to untrusted parties and is NOT RECOMMENDED. If there is no trust relationship, the RFC strongly recommends deleting the location information.

It also warns that using multiple locations together with loc-src may cause compatibility issues, and that hop-by-hop TLS protects against eavesdropping in transit but exposes the information to every SIP intermediary on the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Only share the name tags with people you trust. If you are not sure who will read them, throw the notes away rather than hand them over.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA added a new SIP header field parameter to the Header Field Parameters and Parameter Values subregistry (created by RFC 3968) of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Parameters registry. The entry is: header field Geolocation, parameter name loc-src, predefined values: none, reference RFC 8787.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of allowed name-tag words got one new word added: loc-src.
